claims.text: Adding a few weight percent of a self-lubricating-phase-forming dopant to CoCrFeNi will maintain low friction and reduced wear from 25 to 800 °C.
The dopant can be homogenized into the alloy melt or powder mixture before consolidation.
Sliding-induced thermal and mechanical stresses cause the distributed dopant to segregate to the sliding interface.
The segregated dopant forms a continuous interfacial film during sliding.
The interfacial film is a lubricious compound, likely an oxide or another low-shear phase.
The lubricious film protects the underlying alloy from direct asperity contact.
Sliding-induced local heating activates diffusion of the dopant to the surface.
At the surface, the dopant reacts with environmental oxygen to produce a stable, self-replenishing lubricious phase.
The lubricious phase lowers friction by reducing interfacial shear.
At lower temperatures, discrete patches of the film form and lower friction.
At higher temperatures up to 800 °C, faster reaction kinetics permit formation of a continuous film.
The continuous film reduces wear by limiting direct metal-to-metal contact.
Relative to unmodified CoCrFeNi, the doped alloy will have a significantly lower steady-state coefficient of friction throughout 25–800 °C.
Relative to unmodified CoCrFeNi, the doped alloy will have lower wear rates throughout 25–800 °C.
The doped alloy will exhibit more stable tribological performance under variable loads.
Conventional CoCrFeNi typically exhibits elevated friction and accelerated wear as temperature increases.
The proposed effect depends on an oxidizing environment that supports formation of the lubricious phase.
Excessive dopant concentration may cause adverse microstructural effects and limit efficacy.
